samples.task_summary: Predict whether a respondent has high blood pressure from BRFSS survey features using signals that should generalize across states and years.

scores.rationale: Age is a strong, stable risk factor for hypertension across domains.
Diet quality has some stable association with blood pressure, but this single fruit item is a weak proxy.
Vegetable intake is modestly predictive in a stable way, though noisy and indirect.
Alcohol use can relate to blood pressure, but self-report is noisy and effects are weaker than core clinical factors.
Binge drinking is somewhat relevant to hypertension risk, but likely sparse and noisy.
Physical inactivity is a broadly stable cardiovascular risk marker with moderate usefulness.
Smoking history is a general health risk marker, but its relationship to blood pressure is indirect and not highly specific.
Current smoking status may capture lifestyle risk, though it is less directly tied to hypertension than age or obesity-related factors.
Skin cancer is unlikely to be causally related to blood pressure and may reflect age or healthcare access shortcuts.
Other cancer history is mostly an age/healthcare proxy and not a stable direct predictor of hypertension.
Diabetes is a strong, stable comorbidity associated with hypertension and general cardiometabolic risk.
Poverty can correlate with chronic disease burden and access to care, but it is a demographic shortcut and less directly causal.
Employment status captures age and socioeconomic health differences, but is a brittle proxy rather than a direct risk factor.
Survey year may absorb temporal drift, but it is not a stable semantic predictor and can overfit domain shift.
State is a domain identifier with strong risk of capturing site-specific artifacts rather than generalizable physiology.
Difficulty affording care may reflect untreated chronic illness, but it is also a healthcare-access shortcut and not specific.
Race is a sensitive demographic proxy that may encode structural confounding and domain-specific disparities more than stable biology.
Sex has some stable association with hypertension prevalence, but the effect is moderate and can interact with other factors.

samples.task_summary: Predicting blood pressure-related outcome from BRFSS survey responses, emphasizing features that reflect stable health risk factors and behaviors across domains.

scores.rationale: Age is one of the strongest stable predictors of hypertension and blood pressure risk.
Dietary fruit intake is plausibly related to cardiovascular health, but the signal is usually modest and noisy.
Vegetable intake is a reasonable lifestyle proxy for blood pressure risk, though typically weak and self-reported.
Alcohol consumption can affect blood pressure, but weekly quantity is noisy and often weakly predictive.
Binge drinking captures heavier alcohol use and may relate to blood pressure, but it is still self-reported and unstable.
Physical activity is a broadly stable cardiovascular risk factor and likely useful across domains.
Lifetime smoking history is a durable health risk marker, though less directly tied to blood pressure than age or activity.
Current smoking status is relevant to cardiovascular risk, but self-report and category ambiguity limit stability.
Skin cancer is unlikely to be causally related to blood pressure and may mostly reflect age or healthcare access.
Other cancer history is a weak proxy for age and health burden, but not a robust direct predictor.
Diabetes is a strong, stable comorbidity associated with hypertension and metabolic risk.
Poverty is a stable social determinant linked to chronic disease risk, but it is also a demographic shortcut and less direct.
Employment status can correlate with age, disability, and socioeconomic status, but it is an indirect and domain-sensitive proxy.
Survey year is a domain identifier and can encode dataset shift rather than stable physiology, so it should be heavily downweighted.
State can capture regional health differences, but it is a brittle geographic shortcut and may not generalize well.
Cost-related care avoidance reflects access and chronic disease burden, but it is an indirect and potentially shift-sensitive proxy.
Race is a sensitive demographic variable that may correlate with health disparities, but it is a shortcut and not a stable causal feature.
Sex is a modestly relevant biological factor for blood pressure, though its effect is smaller than age or diabetes.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether a respondent has high blood pressure from BRFSS survey features, emphasizing stable health-risk predictors over domain-specific shortcuts.

scores.rationale: Strong, stable risk factor for hypertension and broadly predictive across domains.
Diet relates to cardiovascular risk, but this single item is noisy and weakly specific.
General dietary pattern can matter, but this coarse measure is only modestly informative.
Alcohol intake can affect blood pressure, though self-report noise and weak marginal signal limit usefulness.
Binge drinking is a plausible cardiovascular risk marker, but still fairly indirect and noisy.
Physical inactivity is a stable health-risk correlate and reasonably predictive of hypertension.
Smoking history is a general cardiovascular risk factor, but less directly tied to blood pressure than age or diabetes.
Current smoking status adds some risk information, but is self-reported and only moderately useful.
Skin cancer is unlikely to be causally related and may mostly reflect age or healthcare access noise.
Other cancer history is weakly related at best and likely acts mostly as an age/health proxy.
Diabetes is a strong, stable comorbidity and major hypertension risk marker.
Socioeconomic hardship can correlate with chronic disease burden, but may be confounded and less stable across domains.
Employment status captures age and health status indirectly, but is a brittle demographic shortcut.
Survey year can capture temporal drift but is not a semantic health predictor and may encode dataset artifacts.
State is a classic domain identifier and likely captures sampling or policy artifacts rather than stable physiology.
Cost-related care avoidance reflects access and chronic disease burden, with some stable but indirect predictive value.
Race can correlate with health disparities but is a sensitive shortcut and often unstable across domains.
Sex has some epidemiologic association with hypertension, but the effect is modest and can be a demographic shortcut.
